items.explanation: Cheap long-distance freight is what let producers sell across the continent — the physical basis of a national market. Railroads carried farm products; they did not end farming. Railroads remained private; Populists demanded public ownership but lost. Factory production grew alongside rail access.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — railroad track grew from about 35,000 miles in 1865 to over 190,000 by 1900

option_explanations.A: Railroads carried farm products to market; farming continued and expanded.
option_explanations.B: Railroads stayed private; Populist demands for public ownership failed.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The rail network made a continent-wide national market possible.
option_explanations.D: Factory production grew with rail access; it did not decline.

options: (A) the end of farming, as railroads replaced agriculture as the nation's principal economic base
(B) government ownership of all American industry, with Washington directly managing the operations of every firm
(C) a national market, in which goods produced in one region could be sold cheaply across the continent
(D) a sharp decline in factory production across the industrial regions
items.stem: Between 1865 and 1900, American railroad track grew from about 35,000 miles to more than 190,000 miles. This expansion most directly made possible...

items.explanation: The cartoon shows the artist's view that corporate interests dominated the Senate — evidence of how big business's political power was perceived. It shows lobbyists present and powerful, not senators refusing to meet them, and not corporations ignoring Washington. But a cartoon expresses an opinion; it cannot prove that any individual senator took a bribe — that overreads what this kind of source can establish.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — trusts, holding companies... built empires + §What the exam tests — government's pro-business stance + PD cartoon (Puck, 1889)

option_explanations.A: The image shows lobbyists looming over willing senators — the opposite of refusal.
option_explanations.B: A cartoon shows the artist's opinion; it cannot prove individual acts of bribery.
option_explanations.C: The cartoon's whole point is that corporations cared deeply about federal policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The cartoon is evidence that corporate influence over government was widely perceived.

options: (A) Senators of the era refused to meet with any business leaders or lobbyists.
(B) The cartoon proves that every senator shown was personally bribed by corporations.
(C) Corporations had no interest in federal policy and ignored Washington entirely.
(D) Large corporations exercised great influence over the federal government.
items.stem: This 1889 Puck cartoon, 'The Bosses of the Senate,' shows corporate lobbyists looming over senators in the Capitol. As historical evidence, the cartoon best supports which claim about the Gilded Age?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Bosses of the Senate,' cartoon by Joseph Keppler, Puck magazine, 1889, showing corporate lobbyists towering over U.S. senators.

items.explanation: Buying competitors at the same stage of production (refining) is horizontal integration — Rockefeller's method. Vertical integration means controlling successive stages from raw material to finished product, as Carnegie did in steel. A labor union organizes workers. The Homestead Act gave western land to settlers.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Vertical / horizontal integration — buying out rivals (Rockefeller) + §The story — Standard Oil, 1870

option_explanations.A: Correct. Buying up rival refineries — competitors at the same stage — is horizontal integration.
option_explanations.B: Vertical integration is controlling successive stages from raw material to product; that was Carnegie's steel method.
option_explanations.C: A labor union organizes workers, not companies.
option_explanations.D: The Homestead Act granted western land to settlers; it has nothing to do with oil refining.

options: (A) horizontal integration — combining with competitors at the same stage
(B) vertical integration — controlling every stage from raw material to finished sale
(C) a labor union — an organization of workers bargaining with employers
(D) the Homestead Act — the law granting western land to settlers
items.stem: John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil, founded in 1870, grew largely by buying up rival oil refineries. This strategy is an example of...

items.explanation: Trusts existed to kill competition and fix prices — Standard Oil is the textbook example. They did the opposite of increasing competition. They were combinations of companies, not worker organizations. The Sherman Act outlawed restraints of trade but was weakly enforced against big business at first, so trusts thrived after 1890.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Trust — Combination of companies under one board to kill competition and fix prices (e.g., Standard Oil) + Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) — weakly enforced against big business at first

option_explanations.A: Trusts were designed to eliminate competition, not increase it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Trusts combined firms to limit competition and control prices.
option_explanations.C: Trusts combined companies; unions organized workers.
option_explanations.D: The Sherman Act was weakly enforced at first, so trusts continued to thrive after 1890.

options: (A) Trusts were designed to increase competition among small businesses by breaking up monopolies.
(B) Trusts reduced competition and gave their organizers power over prices, as with Standard Oil.
(C) Trusts were labor organizations that negotiated higher wages for their worker members.
(D) Trusts were quickly destroyed by the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 after its passage.
items.stem: A trust combined competing companies under a single board of directors. Which statement about trusts is best supported by the historical record of the Gilded Age?

items.explanation: A law against monopolies that the government barely used against monopolists shows where the government's sympathies lay: the Gilded Age federal government was generally pro-business, not neutral. It was not trying to destroy corporations. Trusts flourished after 1890; they had not disappeared. Courts of the era were hostile to unions, not their defenders.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) — weakly enforced against big business at first + §What the exam tests — government's pro-business stance; Government was not neutral

option_explanations.A: The government was not trying to destroy corporations; it left them largely alone.
option_explanations.B: Trusts flourished after 1890 — they had not disappeared.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Weak enforcement of an anti-monopoly law reveals a pro-business government.
option_explanations.D: Courts in this era were hostile to unions, not their defenders.

options: (A) the federal government's determination to destroy every large corporation in the country
(B) the fact that trusts had already disappeared entirely by the year 1890
(C) the federal government's generally pro-business stance during the Gilded Age
(D) the Supreme Court's consistent defense of labor unions against employers

items.explanation: The photograph shows Edison as the public face of invention, but the money followed organization: raising capital, integrating production, and dominating markets. Edison himself sought profit and held many patents, so the first option is wrong, and the patent system protected inventors' claims rather than barring their profits. Patents were private property, not government-owned.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — 'who controlled the new economy'; vertical/horizontal integration; trusts — interpretive synthesis flagged for audit + PD photograph, 1878 (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Edison pursued profit energetically and held many patents; inventors wanted money.
option_explanations.B: The patent system protected inventors' legal claims; it did not bar their profits.
option_explanations.C: Patents were private property held by inventors and companies, not the government.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Organizing capital, production, and markets at scale captured more wealth than inventing alone.

options: (A) Inventors generally refused to accept money for their work, preferring pure scientific inquiry to commercial gain.
(B) The patent system legally barred inventors from earning profits on their own inventions.
(C) The federal government owned all important patents of the era and controlled their use.
(D) Organizing capital, production, and markets on a large scale captured more wealth than inventing alone.
items.stem: This 1878 photograph shows Thomas Edison with his phonograph. Edison was a celebrated inventor, yet the era's greatest fortunes went to business organizers like Carnegie and Rockefeller rather than to inventors. This contrast best illustrates which feature of Gilded Age capitalism?

items.explanation: Instant voice communication across distance let headquarters direct branch offices, factories, and salesmen — the coordination a national-scale company required. Telephones carry information, not freight, so they could not replace railroads. Businesses were among the earliest and heaviest telephone users. Paperwork grew with corporate size; the phone did not eliminate records.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Bell's telephone (1876) 'rewired daily life'; business-coordination effect is general knowledge — flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Telephones carry information, not freight; they could not replace railroads.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Instant long-distance coordination made national-scale management practical.
option_explanations.C: Businesses were among the first major telephone customers.
option_explanations.D: Corporate paperwork grew with business size; the telephone did not eliminate records.

options: (A) replaced the railroad as the main way to move goods between distant cities, towns, and farming regions alike
(B) let managers coordinate distant operations instantly, making national-scale companies practical to run
(C) was used only in private homes and had no real business purpose for companies of any size
(D) eliminated the need for written business records in corporate offices
items.stem: Bell's telephone (1876) 'rewired daily life.' For businesses, the telephone's most important effect was that it...

items.explanation: Large corporations ran on paper: orders, invoices, correspondence, records. The typewriter sped paperwork and the telephone sped messages — together they made managing big organizations feasible. Offices hired more clerks, not fewer. These were communication tools, unrelated to rail travel. Managing factories grew more complex, not unnecessary.
items.fact_source: PD image (Sholes typewriter, manufactured from 1874) for the date; office-adoption claim is general knowledge — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Offices hired more clerks and typists as paperwork grew, not fewer.
option_explanations.B: Communication tools had nothing to do with railroad travel.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Faster paperwork and faster messages made large-scale corporate management possible.
option_explanations.D: Management grew more elaborate as firms grew larger, not unnecessary.

options: (A) eliminating the need for office workers by fully automating all paperwork and business correspondence tasks
(B) ending the use of the railroad for business travel between distant cities and towns
(C) making it possible to handle paperwork and communication at the scale large corporations required
(D) allowing factories to run without managers or any supervision at all
items.stem: The typewriter, first manufactured commercially in the 1870s, spread through business offices in the 1880s and 1890s. Like the telephone, it changed business mainly by...

items.explanation: The ICC was the first federal railroad regulation, created after farmers — squeezed between falling crop prices and freight rates they couldn't control — won state rate laws and demanded federal action. It regulated railroads; it did not free them from oversight. Standard Oil's breakup came decades later and concerned oil, not railroads. It addressed rates, not labor rights.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Interstate Commerce Act (1887) — Created the ICC, the first federal regulation of railroads + §The story — farmers squeezed between falling crop prices and railroad freight rates they could not control

option_explanations.A: The Act imposed regulation; it did not grant freedom from it.
option_explanations.B: Standard Oil was broken up decades later, in 1911 — and it was an oil company, not a railroad.
option_explanations.C: The ICC regulated railroad rates, not labor rights.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The ICC was the first federal railroad regulation, answering farmers' grievances over rates.

options: (A) a law that gave railroad companies complete and permanent freedom from all government regulation and oversight
(B) a measure that broke Standard Oil into separate competing companies
(C) a labor law protecting railroad workers' right to strike for higher pay
(D) the first federal attempt to regulate railroads, answering farmers' anger over rates they could not control
items.stem: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC). The ICC is best understood as...

items.explanation: The industrialists' case rested on growth, lower prices, and innovation; the critics' case rested on wages, hours, debt, and slums — the gap between owners and everyone else. Defenders did not claim wages rose for all; industry stayed private, not government-owned; and nobody disputes that the economy grew enormously.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — 'Prices fell and output soared, but so did the gap between owners and everyone else' + §What the exam tests — Comparison: the Gilded Age economy — who benefited?

option_explanations.A: Correct. Each side's evidence matches: growth and prices for defenders, the owner-worker gap for critics.
option_explanations.B: Defenders cited output and prices, not universal wage gains; critics cited conditions, not falling prices.
option_explanations.C: Industry remained private; no government ownership existed to defend.
option_explanations.D: Both sides agreed the economy grew enormously; they disagreed about who benefited.

options: (A) Defenders cite falling prices and soaring output; critics cite the widening gap between owners and everyone else.
(B) Defenders point to rising wages for all workers, while critics point to falling prices hurting indebted farmers.
(C) Defenders point to government ownership of industry, while critics point to the harmful effects of immigration.
(D) Both sides agree that the economy shrank badly in this period, and they disagree only about the underlying reasons.
items.stem: Historians debate who benefited from the Gilded Age economy. Which pairing best matches each side's evidence?
